Accusplit is an American manufacturer of handheld electronic stopwatches and timers, based in
Pleasanton, California. Its first model, the Harper Accusplit I, was advertised to swimmers in
1973, and its Accusplit 760 of 1978 stored lap splits in memory for recall after a race. The
company says the brand began in 1972 with the first handheld digital stopwatch.[^sw7304][^sw7809][^cat2018]
Accusplit has advertised to swim coaches and lane timers since the 1970s, and from 1992 it
sponsored a national high school relay championship.[^sw9208][^sw9608]

## History

This section follows the brand through its makers and owners as the sources record them.

### Harper Accusplit

The Accusplit I first appeared in Swimming World in April 1973, sold through TAFCO, the mail-order
arm of the magazine Track & Field News, at a list price of $199. The advertisement presented it
as a replacement for the mechanical stopwatch: a quartz-controlled digital display showed
times to 0.01 s, and a "Harper Split" function showed each lap time directly, so a coach no
longer had to subtract cumulative splits by hand. It ran on four C cells.[^sw7304] The advertisements do not name the
maker in full; a collector's history and a museum catalog identify it as
[Harper Time & Electronics](harper-time-electronics.md).[^museum] A cheaper component allowed a large price cut in early 1974, and the
Accusplit III followed in June 1974 and the Accusplit II, at $99.50, by August.[^sw7402][^sw7406][^sw7408]

### Siliconix

In October 1975 an Accusplit dealer announced that the watch was being redesigned and built by
[Siliconix](siliconix.md), a semiconductor company, which gave it a two-year guarantee.[^sw7510] Early the next
year [Recreonics](recreonics.md), Siliconix's national distributor in the aquatics market, advertised two
Siliconix stopwatches, the ET 100 and ET 110, as coming from the makers of the Accusplit.[^sw7602]
The sources do not say how the Accusplit name passed from Harper to Siliconix, or from Siliconix
to the company that later traded as Accusplit, Inc.

### Accusplit, Inc.

Accusplit's memory stopwatch followed in 1978. The 760, advertised from September of that year,
recorded splits as they were taken and displayed them after the race; the advertisement claimed
it was the only stopwatch then on sale with that feature.[^sw7809] W. Ron Sutton, later the
company's chief executive and described on its website as its founder, is credited by Accusplit
with the invention. The company dates it to 1977, during development, in one place and to 1978
in another.[^about][^cat2018]

By February 1981 Accusplit had its own address, 2290A Ringwood Avenue, San Jose, and was the
exclusive distributor of [Maric](../equipment/common/pace-clock/maric-paceclox.md) pace clocks.[^sw8102]
It traded as Accusplit, Inc. from the same address into the 1990s, adopted the tagline "The
Stopwatch Company of America" by 1993, and announced its website in 1996.[^sw9112][^sw9304][^sw9609]
In 1992 and 1993 the [Cronus](cronus.md) stopwatch brand was also advertised from the Ringwood Avenue
address and Accusplit's dealer telephone number.[^cronus92]
Its 2018 catalog gives an address in Pleasanton, California.[^cat2018] From 1983 the company also
worked with the Kato family in Japan on pedometers, which became a second product line.[^about]

### The first-stopwatch claim

Accusplit says it invented the first handheld digital stopwatch in 1972.[^about][^cat2018] Heuer
makes the same claim for its Microsplit 800 of 1972.[^heuer] Neither claim has been checked against
an independent record. The earliest Accusplit advertisement found is from April 1973, and the
company's own anniversary advertising of the 1990s counts 1973 as its first year.[^sw7304][^sw9608]

## Products

This section lists the stopwatch lines in the order they appeared; prices are as advertised.

| Model or series | First advertised | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Accusplit I | April 1973 | Quartz digital display to 0.01 s; Harper Split lap function; four C cells; $199 list[^sw7304] |
| Accusplit III | June 1974 | $149.50 in 1975–1976[^sw7406][^sw7510] |
| Accusplit II | August 1974 | $99.50[^sw7408] |
| 760 | September 1978 | First memory model: stores splits for recall; $79.95[^sw7809][^sw7908] |
| 740, 780, 725, 705 | 1978–1979 | 740 keeps the last four cumulative splits; 780 adds sequential splits; 725 has a split and no memory; 705 has time-out and no split[^sw7908][^sw7911] |
| XP Series (605XP, 725XP, 735XP, 760XP, 920XP) | August 1981 | Replaceable timing module that a dealer could exchange on the spot; 735XP dual split, 1983[^sw8109][^st8305] |
| 790XM | February 1984 | Dual display, 12 memories; $99.95[^sw8402] |
| X3 Series, 760X3 | 1991–1992 | Water-resistant; 760X3 with 100 memories[^sw9112][^sw9208] |
| Ambassador 50 | 1993 | 50 dual "Turbo" split memories; later with a stroke-rate function[^sw9309][^sw0010] |

The company also sold a pocket game timer (model 170, 1983), digital sportswatches with countdown
interval functions (920XP, 930XP), and, from 1981, 20 in and 30 in battery pace clocks, the 320 and
330B.[^st8305][^st8208][^sw8607][^sw8106] The pace clocks match the Maric clocks that Accusplit distributed,
in size, numeral height and battery life.[^sw8102][^sw8106] The current range includes the AX and
Survivor stopwatch lines, pedometers, and a 12 in analog lane timer intended for swim training.[^cat2018]

## In swim timing

Handheld stopwatches are the manual layer of swim timing: lane timers run them as the backup to
touchpads, and coaches use them for splits in training and at meets. Accusplit's advertising was
aimed at both uses. The 1973 Accusplit I was sold on the problem of reading relay legs and lap
times without subtraction, and the 760 on letting a coach or timer record all four legs of a relay
while still watching the takeovers. The 760 advertisements of 1978 and 1979 also promoted it for
official lane timing.[^sw7304][^sw7809] Accusplit's relay advertising of the 1990s traced its "relay tradition" back to
the memory stopwatch of 1978.[^sw9208]

## In competition

The Accusplit High School Relay Championships, sponsored by the company, were a "mythical meet"
that scored high school relay results from across the United States; 45 schools scored in 1996.
The first results were published in 1992, and the ninth edition was announced in 2000.[^sw9208][^sw9608][^sw0008]
From 1993 Richard Quick, who led the US women's Olympic swimming team in 1996, endorsed the
Ambassador series, and sales were linked to a Special Olympics coach and buddy recruitment
fund.[^sw9309][^sw0003] The company describes itself as an official supplier to the 1996
Atlanta Olympic Games.[^about]
